- HR Spotlight


# Caleb Iwuoha on the Personal Cost of Building Acecore


- Great G. Ufford


- November 23, 2026


Table of Contents


Toggle


Caleb nearly missed his chance to pitch at TechCabal Battlefield. He was stuck in Lagos traffic on his way to the National Theatre.


With time running out, he stopped a soldier on his bike and negotiated a price to the venue. He arrived tense, with three minutes to explain years of work.


By the time he finished, he was convinced he had done badly. It was a familiar feeling for Caleb.


He had already faced more than 100 rejections that year. This was his third attempt at the competition. But Caleb has learnt something about rejection. When one opportunity doesn’t work out, he moves on to the next.


Our latest Founders Spotlight features Caleb Iwuoha, founder of Acecore. His company makes clean energy hardware and came from personal loss, hard choices, and people who chose to stay.


##


The day everything changed


On June 13, 2024, Caleb’s father went in for cancer surgery. During the operation, the hospital lost power. Caleb says the outage contributed to a medical error.


His father died in December that year. Caleb had already made up his mind about building clean energy products in Nigeria.


COVID-19 had shown him the risks of relying on imported equipment. But losing his father made the problem much more personal.


He knew what unreliable power could cost a business. Now, he had experienced what could happen when the power went out during a medical procedure.
Losing his father gave him another reason to keep building.


##


Why starting in Port Harcourt mattered to him


Caleb knew that Lagos offered better access to investors and startup networks. He still chose to build Acecore in Port Harcourt.
He wanted talented people in Rivers State to find jobs close to home.


He also believed that a company making hardware didn’t need to be based in Lagos to succeed. There was another reason he had to make do with what was available.


He had no money to set up a factory, so he started in his father’s garage. Caleb began researching the business during his industrial training year in 2021.


He launched the brand in 2022, while he was still a student. He had no savings, no revenue, and little experience running a company.


Later, Acecore secured funding. He expanded the factory into the family compound. The factory had grown, but building hardware in Nigeria brought new problems. The people who believed enough to stay.


At some point, Caleb began asking himself why he had chosen such a difficult business. Hardware took time and money to build. Finding the right engineers was another challenge.


Skilled hardware engineers were much harder to find than software engineers and when the company wasn’t making money, some people left. He remembers one hardware engineer who decided to quit.


Caleb offered to change his contract. He was willing to meet whatever terms would make the engineer stay. The engineer still left.


Caleb had to find another way to keep the work going, so he started learning more of the technical work himself. He began doing the coding, design, and manufacturing work himself.


But not everyone walked away.


One of his co-founders left a paying job in Lagos and moved to Port Harcourt to build Acecore. Another turned down an opportunity to travel abroad. Caleb said some of his admin staff worked for four years without pay. Other team members made difficult choices too.


Caleb says his chief software engineer turned down opportunities at Google and Facebook. His finance lead, Colin, also passed on roles at major Nigerian energy companies. He also postponed plans to pursue a PhD at MIT so he could continue building the company.


He describes the kind of people willing to take these risks as “crazy.” But he speaks about them with gratitude. He said his faith and co-founder kept him going. When we asked how he keeps people committed to the work, Caleb pointed to leading by example. He recalls working through three nights at the factory without sleep. He wanted his engineers to see the standard of work he expected from them.
It was an exhausting way to work, and the company’s problems didn’t disappear overnight. Still, he had people around him who continued to believe they could make it work.


##


What 100 rejections taught him


Caleb’s approach to rejection started long before his TechCabal win. During his industrial training year (IT), someone gave him an unusual piece of advice. He should apply to 100 companies in sustainable agriculture and prepare to hear “no” from 99 of them.


Caleb took that advice seriously. He stopped seeing every “no” as a setback. That thinking followed him into building Acecore. He tried TechCabal Battlefield twice without success. On his third attempt, he won.
He said he got into Y Combinator after four applications. His experience with the Startup World Cup followed a similar pattern.


In 2023, he didn’t make it through. In 2024, he reached the top 100. By 2025, he was among the three finalists in Germany. And in 2026 alone, Caleb estimates that he has received at least 100 rejections.


His response has become almost routine. When an application fails, he doesn’t spend the rest of the day thinking about it. He looks for the next opportunity and applies again. The advice he received years ago has stayed with him. If he expects to hear “no” many times, one more rejection doesn’t have to be the end of the story.


##


The win he almost missed


Getting to the TechCabal Battlefield stage was difficult enough. Caleb had spent much of the journey worrying about whether he would arrive on time.


Then came the pitch itself. He had prepared to explain Acecore’s hardware, energy management software and other technology. But the three-minute format was different from what he was used to.


He struggled to fit everything into the time he had. He even stuttered during the presentation. When he left the stage, he felt he had performed poorly. By the next day, he had won another pitch at the Nigeria Energy Innovation Challenge. He was ready to move on, and he had other plans for the time TechCabal would announce its winners.


An acquaintance who had watched his Battlefield pitch insisted that he attend. So Caleb went. He sat in the hall with his head down, thinking Acecore might come second or third, at best. Then they announced Acecore as the winner. He won the same competition that turned him down twice.


His first thought was about what the prize money could do for the company. He could hire more engineers.
The one person he wanted to call was his mother. She had listened to him talk about many rejections for years. Now, he finally had good news to share.


##


There’s still so much he wants to build


Caleb has a big ambition for Acecore. He wants to build what he calls the “Tesla and Apple of Africa.”
He admires Apple’s attention to design and Tesla’s approach to innovation. He wants Acecore to make products in Nigeria that can meet those same standards. Not everyone believes that is possible.


Some people question whether Acecore can compete with American companies. Those companies have more money, equipment and experienced engineers. Caleb understands the difference in resources. He has spent years working with little himself.


He had no money when he started, so he worked from his father’s garage. When engineers left, he learned to do some of their work himself. He has also seen people give up better-paying opportunities to help him build. These experiences have shaped how he thinks about what is possible.


After years of trying, Caleb finally had his TechCabal Battlefield win. But even as they announced his name, he was already thinking about the work ahead because there’s still so much he wants to build.
